March 26, 1984
Canada Health Act

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-3, An Act relating to cash contributions by Canada in respect of insured health services provided under provincial health care insurance plans and amounts payable by Canada in respect of extended health care services and to amend and repeal certain Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, and Motion No. 4 (Mr. Halliday).

Mr. Speaker, at one o'clock, when the House took recess, the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) had presented his amendment to Bill C-3. I would now like to summarize for the House the history of Clause 12 as amended by the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, to clarify the reasons for the present form of this Clause in the Bill, the report stage of which is now being considered by the House, and the exact implications of the amendment being proposed by the Hon. Member for Oxford.
Mr. Speaker, the House will recall, and the Hon. Member himself referred to this point, that Mr. Justice Hall has always indicated the inherent duality of eliminating extra-billing, which he proposed, and the need for providing doctors with a framework for negotiations with the provinces which are responsible for setting standards of compensation for insured health services. More specifically, Mr. Speaker, when he appeared before the Committee, Mr. Justice Hall indicated that the binding arbitration procedure which he recommended in his 1980 report should not be imposed through legislation, and should certainly not constitute a fundamental condition for implementing the federal legislation.
Aware of this dilemma, Committee members examined the concept, favoured by Mr. Justice Hall and recommended, much later, by the Canadian Medical Association-I say much later, because originally, the Association did not see the need for it-in order to see to what extent this framework for discussion could be incorporated into the federal legislation, while leaving intact the concept of shared responsibility or jurisdiction, it being understood that health is a provincial responsibility, generally speaking, with respect to providing services, allocating resources, and setting priorities, while federal jurisdiction covered spending powers and a responsibility, taken on twenty-five years ago, for making federal transfer payments, provided the five essential conditions are met.
Now, the concept of reasonable compensation, since that is what we are talking about here, which was in the original 1966
legislation on health care, went as far as the Canadian Government thought it could go in urging participating provinces to ensure that their doctors received "reasonable" compensation, a subjective concept, I agree, which is or was in Bill C-3 as originally introduced in the House, considered at the second reading stage and referred to Committee.
The Committee had to decide, first of all, whether or not this framework for discussion, this framework for negotiations leading to binding arbitration-arbitration, that is, always preceded by negotiations-could be put in the federal legislation without interfering directly with the responsibility of the provinces which, with respect to negotiations, and I was referring earlier to compensation, is not contested. The answer was yes, after lengthy discussions in Committee. We decided that this framework could be incorporated in the federal legislation. The second question, a corollary of the previous one, was to decide whether or not we had to impose, on the ten participating provinces, this framework for discussion and negotiations and, eventually, binding arbitration, within the concept or general framework of reasonable compensation.
The Committee decided: no, we did not want to impose binding arbitration on the provinces but we would leave it up to the provinces to operate within the framework of the negotiations specified and enumerated in paragraph 2 of clause 12 as amended in Committee.
I think that is the basic element which enables us now to reply to the argument and the amendment moved by the Hon. Member for Oxford. Indeed, if subclause (2) is optional-and so it is, obviously-we must check whether or not the proposed amendment nullifies that option. I say it does because subclause (2) provides that, if the provinces and the medical associations involved have signed and agreed on a negotiating formula, the reasonable compensation criterion will be respected. On the other hand, if there is no agreement, the reasonable compensation criterion takes precedence-the subjective criterion which remains and which, in the final analysis, will always leave the Minister of National Health and Welfare free to intervene if necessary and apply the penalties mentioned in clause 14 and the following clauses of the Bill.
Now, what would happen if the amendment of the Hon. Member for Oxford were adopted? By adding the word "only", we would inevitably commit the legal negotiating structure proposed under the reasonable compensation clause. Without legal structure, without agreement among the provinces, the federal Minister would necessarily have to resort to penalties as provided for in the Bill and as the federal Minister is authorized to do pursuant to the Bill. I respect the Hon. Member for Oxford for what he is attempting to do, and I might add that I agree with him that we ought to make sure that Canadian medical practitioners do receive reasonable compensation and have the means to obtain it. But still the basic problem remains unsolved and we have to cut the
March 26, 1984

Gordian knot. Yes or no, does the House want to force the mechanism proposed in the Bill on the provinces?
It is an issue or a problem which is difficult to solve and I would rather not get into a lengthy argument on the delicate balance between the federal presence and the provincial responsibilities in the field of health care, for we all know the conditions of that essential balance. Personally, I would much prefer that the Canadian Government did not force-I repeat, force-the provinces and the medical associations concerned, through the new Canada Health Act, to accept any legal structure whatsoever. In my opinion, that is exactly what would happen if we were to adopt the amendment of the Hon. Member for Oxford.
Although I appreciate what he is attempting to do, that is why I cannot support his amendment since it would force the provinces to accept a structure which the committee made sure would not be compulsory.

Mr. Speaker, this amendment was proposed in committee and there is quite a history behind it. I think it is important, in order to understand what is being proposed, to look at the background of this amendment proposed by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday). It has always been difficult to answer a number of questions on a national health scheme, but one question which has always been front and centre is: How do you establish a national health scheme yet retain professional freedom within that scheme? The definition of professional freedom might have various dimensions or parameters depending on the observer, but what has happened through the years is that a certain equilibrium has been established between the province, represented primarily by the Ministry of Health, the Health Services Commission, and the medical profession, generally represented by a provincial organization or the umbrella body, the Canadian Medical Association.
It is interesting to note that Mr. Justice Hall, in his report studying the health care system, which report was commissioned by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Rosedale (Mr. Crombie) when he was Minister of National Health and Welfare, made two fundamental points. He said that extra billing and user fees had the potential or eroding medicare as Canadians had come to understand it. We can argue about the consultation process, and I am going to get to that on third reading, but for the purpose of this debate the perception of Mr. Justice Hall was that that was a potential problem. However, he never looked at the solution to that problem, as he identified it, in isolation.
He also recognized that the primary focus of the health care system had to be service to Canadians first. In order to have proper service, the health care professionals had to feel not only that they were being fairly treated, but that their professionalism was being recognized. The other half of the argument that he put forward was that if extra billing was either to
Canada Health Act
be outlawed or penalties for its use applied, which could eventually lead to its demise, then there had to be reasonable and fair compensation for the medical profession.
Members can argue that those are two almost irreconcilable points of view. When you add thereto the reality of federal-provincial jurisdictional components and responsibilities, you come up with a very difficult problem to solve, if a solution can be found. That is why, Mr. Speaker, just on that narrow ground, it was our preference that negotiations with the provinces take place before the Canada Health Act is brought in. But that is not what we have been facing over these past few weeks. That being the case, when one comes to the operative words "reasonable compensation", what does it mean and how do you get it?
I said that what is reasonable would vary with the individual. I cannot speak for the Canadian Medical Association, but I know there are a lot of discussions within that organization and their provincial affiliates as to how to address this matter of the established equilibrium being eroded. There was this new factor, that of a penalty being imposed if extra billing continues. I do not know what the legal fees relating to this clause are, Mr. Speaker, but I know that an awful lot of work went into the clause, and so at least in part we addressed the question. I say "in part". What concerns me, if we do not accept this amendment, is this nebulous but real relationship which a professional has to his or her place of work. That is real. I know that the majority of Canadians say they wanted penalties for extra billing, but the existing mechanism had created an understanding, an equilibrium. All the committee tried to do was to restore some mechanism whereby, if the equilibrium, the fairness and reasonableness, is not achievable, then at least the mechanism to try and reach those goals might be set up. I am convinced that if we do not have that kind of mechanism, the medical profession will feel that their professionalism, their training and their service is not recognized adequately. I am not talking about dollars, I am talking about attitude. It is part of professionalism. That is why I think this amendment is so important.
If we were to have that kind of negative attitude toward the system and the manner in which the services are provided and compensated for, who would suffer most? That is the question we have to ask. Is it the medical profession? Is it potentially the Canadian public who needs the service? I am not saying that doctors will automatically try to provide an inferior service, but I think we have to deal with the psychology of the situation and with how a professional views himself or herself. That is the point I am trying to get across. I suggest that the manner in which the Ontario Medical Association puts forward its case does not augur well for the manner in which the problems endemic to the health care system will be resolved.
I do not subscribe to the concept that this is conscription-I want to make that very clear. It is not civilian conscription. If you look at many professional groups, having established a salary and working conditions, that is their contract. But within this system I suggest it would be detrimental to the public if we saw the Canadian medical profession, either by

March 26, 1984
Canada Health Act
their rhetoric, their actions or the actions of this House, being pushed into or moved into a position where they feel that what we often call job action is justified. The greatest hurt would then be inflicted on those Canadians who need health care
services.
It does not do the Canadian Medical Association or health care providers any good, who, through a bargaining mechanism, withdraw their services from the ill. I must admit I do not have a lot of evidence that that kind of action has in fact benefited the profession. Maybe this goes back to my relationship to a profession I was once in. I never felt that job action was a better solution than sitting down around a table and, no matter how long it took, or how frustrating the experience, eventually as adult men and women coming up with an agreement.

Mr. Speaker, I thank Hon. Members for their courtesy. I would like to say, that being the case, I urge Members to once again examine this motion. I believe we have come some distance toward addressing the problems which have been put forward by my colleague and others. I believe that we could strengthen the solution which the committee came up with after hours of hard work. I commend the motion, Mr. Speaker, to the House in order that within months we will not have job action or the potential of job action which would hurt those Canadians who need the service of the medical system.

Mr. Speaker, even though I speak in support of the amendment by the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) I have never accepted the argument which was put forward by the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) that there is some kind of inextricable link between professionalism and extra billing. I have always found it very difficult to understand how the professionalism of one profession, in this case the medical profession, could be so bound up with the ability to extra bill patients when the professionalism of other professions is unrelated to whether or not they are able to bill clients over and above what they are paid through their salary.
Having said that, I would like to say that I have always supported, on behalf of my Party, the recommendation of Justice Hall that the outlawing of extra billing in any particular province go hand in hand with binding arbitration procedures in those provinces. I have stood up in the House on many occasions over the past four years and called on the Minister to do something about the erosion of medicare represented by extra billing. Many times I included in my representations to
her our support for the concept of binding arbitration. Therefore, I have no problem supporting an amendment which I know has the support of the Canadian Medical Association, a group I am normally not in agreement with. I do not do this out of any affection for their Association, particularly given their most recent activity; I do it in the interest of consistency and in the interest of the position I have taken since the beginning of this debate on the erosion of medicare and how extra billing ought to be eliminated.
In that respect I would submit that we are unlike the other two Parties in the House. We are unlike the Tories who never said boo about extra billing. I invite people to check the record. I invite them to search through Hansard high and low, between the lines, through the lines and around the lines to find out if anyone in the House on behalf of the P.C. Party ever expressed a concern about extra billing before the Canada Health Act was actually tabled and a political judgment was made that the Act would be supported, which is fair enough. We were calling for the elimination of extra billing and for binding arbitration when others were paying no attention at all to extra billing.
This gives me an opportunity to make a general comment which is related to the concern of the Hon. Member for Provencher about professionalism. In recent days with the turning over of the membership list of the Canadian Medical Association to the National Citizens' Coalition, as was reported in the newspapers, and with the full page ads-
The Ontario Medical Association, not the Canadian Medical Association.

I am sorry, the Ontario Medical Association- I stand corrected and the turning over of their membership list to the National Citizens' Coalition and the full page ads taken out by the National Citizens' Coalition against the Canada Health Act. Not only that, but the ads we have seen in the Ottawa area recently, where the monitors are going, "beep, beep, beep" is supposed to be what is happening to medicare as a result of the Canada Health Act. I am known to be a critic of doctors. I do not have high expectations of them, but I have maintained my respect for them as professionals through all the debates we have had from one end of the country to the other, whether in Victoria with the special parliamentary task force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements, or in the committee hearings on the Canada Health Act.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that I think some of the things which have gone on lately have brought shame to the vocational integrity of the medical profession in Canada. I am genuinely, deeply disappointed. There must be thousands of doctors who feel as I do. I certainly hope that is the case. I am confident that is the case. I hope they will make it known to their various leaders that they have had enough of being embarrassed in the way that they have been embarrassed, particularly in recent weeks, by some of the advertisements we have seen in the Ottawa area. It is to pile dishonour upon dishonour to have the National Citizens' Coalition declare itself to be in alliance with the position the doctors have taken.
March 26, 1984

This is a terrible thing, Mr. Speaker. I hope the opportunity will present itself for all right thinking doctors to speak out. They may disagree with this Bill and that is fine. Disagreeing with this Bill is a legitimate political stance as long as one is willing to debate it within the bounds of reasonableness.
We do not know what the effects of the Canada Health Act may be. We do not know whether the penalties will have the desired effect in Ontario. We are only talking about what may happen. Provinces still have the freedom to do as they wish with regard to extra billing. Referring to that as civilian conscription, talking about having heart surgery done by civil servants, is the kind of tactics, unreasonableness and fear mongering that is completely unacceptable.
I hope that this debate might mark the beginning of a reform movement within the medical profession itself. I hope that the "old boys' club" could be broken up so that new doctors with fresh ideas of how the medical profession works in greater harmony with other health care practitioners and more accountability to the community might say that they cannot afford to let those in the Canadian Medical Association or Ontario Medical Association represent them throughout the country because they are doing a poor job. I hope that small group within those associations is doing a poor job in speaking for ordinary doctors who often work under difficult circumstances to do their best to care for their patients. Nobody has denied that. I hope the CMA and the OMA are doing a poor job of representing those ordinary doctors in the sense that I hope they are not representative of the views of ordinary people, as we have discovered in our travels throughout the country.
I am disappointed by the medical profession and its participation in this debate. One receives messages from them that are incoherent and quite childish, referring to political fraud. But having said that, I support this amendment because in spite of the doctors, I support fairness for them and a balanced approach to the elimination of extra billing.
I was one of the first to suggest in committee that without an amendment such as that proposed by the Hon. Member for Oxford the legislation would not meet the legitimate needs for some kind of balance as expressed by the doctors. If the Government does not support the amendment it should remove the Conservatives' amendment altogether, since it is merely a poetic or rhetorical addition to the Bill. It does not require anything of the provinces.
It is a statement.

Perhaps it is. I am simply trying to point out the legal meaninglessness of it. I am acceptable to arguments for leaving it in but I am simply saying that it does not have much effect as it is. It may be legitimately argued that it should be left in because it has some symbolic effect, similar to the amendment for the health care practitioner. In that respect, perhaps it would be better to leave it in.
Canada Health Act
The provinces do not seem to understand the purpose of the amendment, which is unusual, because usually there is close communication between the CMA and the provinces. The provinces are concerned that the amendment in its present form, without the subamendment by the Hon. Member for Oxford, is far too aggressive and places them in a difficult position. This shows a political irony because the Progressive Conservative Member for Oxford is suggesting that we should be more intrusive. That does not disturb me because I have always wanted the federal Government to be more intrusive in the case of medicare and the preservation of its principles. I am pleased to welcome the Hon. Member for Oxford aboard and to express my happiness that he finally realizes the responsibility of the federal Government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, having listened to the oration by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), I am not sure whether his support is an advantage or disadvantage. I will have to weigh what he said very carefully.
In any event, I would like to speak briefly to the amendment that has been put forward by my colleague for Oxford (Mr. Halliday) because Clause 12(2), as it exists in the Bill before us, is in itself an amendment. The words of subsection 2 have been agreed to in committee although they were not the first preference of the Conservative Party members who sat on the committee on Health and Welfare.
The amendment that was put forward in committee by my colleague for Provencher (Mr. Epp) would have provided a much firmer and more equitable system of reasonable compensation than we have before us today. I wish that the Government, in recognizing that there had to be a balance between the removal of extra billing and the provision of a regular schedule of fees for the medical profession, would have accepted what my colleague put forward. If it had done so, the necessity for the amendment by the member for Oxford would have been eliminated.
The amendment by the Member for Provencher would have indicated to the doctors, the provinces and other interested parties that the necessary equality has been carried out in order to make the entire system work. While we have accepted the fact that there should be no extra billing, we have provided a mechanism whereby medical practitioners can be assured of reasonable compensation for the services which they so willingly and devotedly give to Canadians. It would have been a proper step to take, but it was not accepted. Instead, we are faced with the Government's amendment to Clause 12(2) as it is now before us. That amendment embodies the concept of what my colleague from Provencher put before the committee but does not have the strength and therefore, in my view, will not prove satisfactory in the long run.
There are inherent weaknesses in the amendment which the Government has incorporated in this Clause of the Bill. It is in that light that the Hon. Member for Oxford sought to strengthen the Bill, if only minimally. Nevertheless, that

March 26, 1984
Canada Health Act
amendment does bring some strength and depth to the procedure of providing for reasonable compensation that the present amendment lacks.
When I spoke to other amendments before the House this morning, I talked rather encouragingly-something I do not always do-about the way the Minister and some of her colleagues had been generous enough to at least accept the concept of the amendment, if not the wording, that had been put forward by opposition Parties in committee. They took some steps toward meeting what we thought were those qualities of fairness and justice that were so clearly delineated by Mr. Justice Hall. However, the Government was not totally receptive.
One of the advantages of the report stage of any Bill is that it gives the Government the opportunity for sober second thought. It is not only the other place that has that opportunity, it is provided in our rules and procedures for the Government to come to that stage itself.
1 believe that this amendment allows the Government to take a second look at the proposals it has put forward. I am sure that in the light of sober second thought the Minister will see the reasonableness of this amendment, and the need for it. I know that later this day she will want to advise her colleagues that this very small but very important amendment should be incorporated into the Bill because it would strengthen the mechanism that we are now introducing. That would reassure many people who are concerned about the lack of any kind of balance in the Bill. It would reassure them that there is a willingness to see that these difficulties are met, and that in the long run once again we will have a better Bill.
I commend the amendment to the Minister. I am sure she will give it that degree of sober second thought that I have urged upon her. I will be only too happy to see her and members of her party stand in their places later today and indicate their support for this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, may I commend at the outset to Hon. Members in this House and to those in the press gallery a reading of the first draft of Bill C-3, the Health Care Act. It went through the proceedings of this House up to and including second reading. I would like Hon. Members to compare that draft with the Bill we have before us this afternoon. After that careful consideration if they do not come to the conclusion that major surgery was done on the Bill, and I refer specifically to clauses 3 and 4 being the objectives and the purposes of the Bill, I would then ask them to refer to clause 12. Just before someone says it is not relevant to the issue let me state that clause 12 itself contains such words as "adequacy of funding" for hospital care, and "reasonableness" of remuneration to medical prac-tioners in the delivery of medicare.
Those words were part of the first draft and part of the indication by this Government when it introduced Bill C-3 that there was going to be a new era in medicare. Witnesses, one
after another, came before the standing committee indicating that, yes, while Bill C-3 was limited in its approach, this was simply phase one or stage one to a second or third stage which might quickly follow.
They were disillusioned after they saw the amendments that were introduced by Government Members and the changes that were made to the Bill itself. I supported the continuation of the term adequacy of funding for hospitals. But that was eliminated. The Government did not, and I am glad it did not introduce any resolution with respect to eliminating the word "reasonableness" for medical compensation to our practioners.
The Hon. Mr. Justice Hall, who has often been referred to as the founder of medicare in this country, commissioned as he was to conduct a review ten years after the implementation of medicare, did indicate there was a potential for erosion through user fees and extra billing. He said in his report, and he said during the committee's deliberations, that it was a potential only, that there was no present erosion to the degree that we were not first in the world with respect to medicare, but it had a potential and that, therefore, something should be done about it.
Having regard to suggestions about disturbing, or failing to disturb the equilibrium, obviously that distinguished jurist had in mind that if you eliminate extra billing there has to be something else in its place to protect the income of medical practioners. He suggested as part of that balance that there be compulsory arbitration. First reading of Bill C-3 did not contain any such provision of arbitration or a compensating process. Only after committee deliberation was clause 12(2) introduced, having to do with that arbitration process.
I suggest that even with the introduction of that arbitration process there is no guarantee the Government can deliver on its clause 12 "reasonableness" of compensation if there is no agreement reached between the provinces and the medical profession in each of those provinces, because the default clauses, clauses 14 and 15, do not apply to provisions of this nature. They only apply to whether it is dollar for dollar adjustment of block funding. They only apply where there has been, perhaps, some extra billing by a province or an abuse, if you call it that, with respect to user fees. There is no way that the federal government can guarantee our medical practioners that reasonableness of income.
It is incumbent upon this House to protect those practioners of medicine as far as we can possibly go. That is one of the reasons our party insisted that there be included in the Bill an arbitration process. If today, or before this Bill is finally given Royal assent, we can protect them even further, it is the duty and the responsibility of Members of this Houe so to do. That was the purpose and the intent of motion No. 4 as introduced by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halli-day). If those medical practioners are not to be adequately compensated here in Canada, then I repeat what I said this morning, that the greatest threat to accessibility of medicare is not through extra billing and user fees, the greatest threat will be the lack of skilled practioners in medicine. That is not a risk which this country nor Canadians should take.
March 26, 1984
Hear, hear!

It becomes incumbent upon us this afternoon to impress upon the Minister the desirability of strengthening clause 12(2) by the inclusion of that single word "only" and the responsibility of the Government will only be eliminated, will only be diminished, if the federal Government sees each province enter into a written binding agreement with its medical practioners that will provide them with reasonable compensation for their efforts.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to take part in this debate and to address the issue raised in Motion No. 4 proposed by the Hon. Member for Oxford (Mr. Halliday). I can understand the Hon. Member for Oxford presenting this kind of an amendment to the House of Commons. It is consistent with his view. He is honest and logical in his view. He has been sincerely concerned about the procedure for compensation and arbitration for the medical profession with or without Bill C-3.
What is very hard to understand, however, is how a party that has, at least up to now, given itself the vocation of not only respecting provincial rights, but defending provincial rights, can be so hypocritical in this kind of situation when it is prescribing, because that will be the effect of the amendment.
The Hon. Member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) says there are only a few words when in fact there is just one word, the word "only". But the effect of inserting the word only in the Bill at this time would be to prescribe to the provinces and to the legislatures of the provinces an arbitration procedure in advance. It would be the Parliament of Canada involving itself in a crude intrusion into the jurisdiction of the provincial legislatures to prescribe an arbitration procedure, not only between two professional groups, which is bad enough, but between professional group and a provincial government in the establishment of a fee schedule. It is pure hypocrisy for a Party to support this kind of amendment, a party that wants people to believe that it respects provincial rights.
There is another reason why I am against this amendment and against prescribing to provincial governments the detailed kind of arbitration procedure set out in Clause 12(l)(c) on page 9 of the Bill. Under a variety of statutes Parliament provides compensation, grants, investment tax credits, loans, loan guarantees and all kinds of assistance to industry or groups in the country without prescribing how their workers are to be compensated.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie) wants to be fair to the medical profession-which is a change of heart-and in this case when Parliament, through spending power, provides money to provincial governments under certain conditions he wants to make sure that there is a reasonable and fair compensation or arbitration procedure. Through IRDP, under the Ministry of Regional Industrial Expansion, and through a variety of other programs we provide assistance
Canada Health Act
to provincial governments, companies or groups and do not require that an arbitration procedure be followed. In fact, in many ways the federal Government allocates money to groups that employ workers who are not unionized, but are at the mercy of provincial labour laws.
This amendment is a crude intrusion into the jurisdiction of provincial legislatures. Therefore, it is not acceptable that Parliament should pass it without the agreement of the provinces. It is also inequitable. It says that in the case of the medical profession Parliament should start prescribing arbitration procedures when giving money to provinces for medical care or hospitalization, but this is not prescribed under other programs where money is given to provincial governments for equalization or post-secondary education, for example. Under federal law, many Departments provide money to groups, individuals, provincial governments and business enterprises.
I think the Progressive Conservative Party should make up its mind; either it wants to respect the spirit of the Constitution, the federal-provincial balance when the federal parliament uses the spending power, or it is going to cater to any group in the country that can mount an effective lobby. I think it is trying to show medical practitioners that it is very sympathetic to them; that it did not want to ban extra billing without the doctors having an arbitration procedure. However, it is not ready to say to the medical profession, "Sorry Messieurs et Mesdames, you missed the opportunity when Mr. Justice Hall brought in his report in 1980, when the Parliamentary Task Force on federal-provincial fiscal arrangements reported in 1981, and when the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin), at the request of the Province of Saskatchewan, offered to define and control extra billing and twin that with a fair compensation system and an arbitration procedure for the medical profession."
At the time the medical profession totally ignored that and determined it was going to fight the issue of extra billing and user fees at the ideological level. It made the political error of thinking it could convince Cabinet and Members of the House that this was a time of so-called neo-conservatism, that the public wanted less government and it could win by stopping political action on the part of Parliament to discourage extra billing and user fees. It is too bad it made a political mistake. It misread public opinion and it misread Parliament.
Now the Conservatives want to say that they would give a little bit when they know very well that if this amendment were adopted it would be a crude intrusion into provincial jurisdiction. Provinces would take the Bill to court and would probably lose in the Supreme Court. Perhaps that is what the Conservatives want. Perhaps they are afraid to face up to the tough decision to discourage extra billing and user fees. Perhaps this is all a plot on their part to make sure that some provincial governments bring the Bill to court. In that case medicare would go down the drain.
In committee the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) proposed an amendment that would have had the same effect as the one now before us. He justified it by saying that if Parliament moves on extra billing and user fees without pro-

March 26, 1984
Canada Health Act
vincial agreement, it should be able to move on the question of arbitration without provincial agreement. What he did not say then, and what he did not say today, is that we are not proceeding legally to ban extra billing or user fees. The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill made that point, however.
Technically and legally speaking we are not touching the very crucial legal question of extra billing and user fees. What we are doing is putting conditions on moneys that Parliament provides to provinces under its spending power. We are saying that under certain conditions the appropriations to these provinces will be reduced and we are prescribing the extent to which they will be reduced.
The opportunity was there in 1980, it was there in 1981, it was there in 1982 for the provincial governments-with the support of the medical profession if it had seen the writing on the wall-to make sure that Parliament would not move unilaterally in the area of extra billing and user fees unless there was a recommendation, through agreement with the provinces, for an arbitration procedure. The doctors fooled themselves, Mr. Speaker. They made a bad political error and a bad error of judgment. Now they are in the position in some provinces that they do not have any arbitration procedure.
Contrary to the views of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill, I believe that the Government has proposed a meaningful opportunity for the provinces to elect a certain arbitration principle and procedure and that the law would provide that that would satisfy the provision in Clause 12(1 )(c) for reasonable compensation. This is important because it provides a model and a moral impetus, a political impetus, to the medical profession in the provinces to get their provincial governments to agree to an arbitration procedure. I believe that kind of moral pressure on the system is good for Parliament and it is within our rights to do it. It will provide a model that we hope some provinces will adopt right away. I believe that two or three of them will apply it right away, and that will mean that the medical profession will have the tool to pressure those provincial governments politically to make sure that they get some kind of arbitration procedure. They deserve it.

Mr. Speaker, that was an incredible speech. For the Hon. Member to stand up in this House and say that the doctors have made a political mistake is to underline in part what is wrong with the Government's approach to health care in the country. I would prefer-and I think most Canadians would-a doctor capable of diagnosing my gall-bladder problem, my heart problem or my disease. We do not expect doctors to go to university for ten years to study politics. If the health care system is regarded as something necessary to turn doctors into politicians, then I think we have identified one of the key problems of the Government's approach to health care generally.
We are dealing with Clause 12, Mr. Speaker. It begins with the following phrase:
In order to satisfy the criterion respecting accessibility, the health care insurance plan of a province-
A number of subclauses follow. It is a clause dedicated to assuring Canadians access to quality health care. However, does it deal with the issue of accessibility as it may be experienced by a patient? May I suggest to the House that for the most part it totally ignores the problems in the Canadian health care system as they affect the issue of accessibility.
If I were to walk out the front door and get hit by a taxi cab, Mr. Speaker, the first issues of accessibility which would concern me as a patient would be the availability of an ambulance, a hospital bed and a well trained professional to look after me. The problems that exist in the country relating to accessibility are not in the order of paying $5 and having to give up seeing a movie. The problems are the absence of a hopsital bed when needed, the absence of a piece of equipment when needed, and the absence of a medical practitioner when needed.
I have heard the spokesperson for the New Democratic Party say that he does not understand the relationship between the quality of health care provided by a professional person and the fee or income of that professional person. To say that is to live in an environment like that of Alice in Wonderland. We are asking people to commit their lives to health care professions. When they do, what do they face, Mr. Speaker? They face first a long training period. A medical doctor will pay for his education for six to 10 years and gives up income.
When a health care professional graduates, what do we say to him, Mr. Speaker? We say that he should be available to his community 24 hours a day, seven days a week because illness does not respect the clock. Illness is not very pleasant to encounter, neither for the person who is ill nor for the person who cares for that person. We tell health care professionals that we want them to be available 24 hours a day, seven days a week, with their knowledge, expertise and compassion to provide a service to people. We then hear a spokesperson for the Government stand up and talk about labour relations.
Do we want people to enter the health care professions who are more concerned about whether a work day should be seven hours, six hours and 40 minutes or seven hours and 20 minutes; whether a coffee break should be precisely 15 minutes long? Do we really want to apply a labour relations model which was developed for use in factories and assembly line tasks to health care professionals? Do we want to impose that on people who are supposed to be committed, who spend a long time being trained and who professionally upgrade themselves year after year and day after day? Do we want to impose a factory and assembly line model on those people?
When we tell people that they must have a fee schedule, we are telling them that a particular treatment or diagnostic procedure is worth $10, $15 or $22. When talking to patients, we frequently hear them say things like: "Yes, I got in to see my doctor. Sometimes I waited an hour, sometimes I waited two hours but the one thing that I do not feel very happy about is that my doctor did not spend enough time with me. I do not
March 26, 1984

really feel comfortable that he knows about all of my symptoms or all of the things that are wrong with me. I am not really sure about the diagnosis so maybe I will have to try and go back and see him in another week or two." Senior citizens in the country will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that 10, 20 or 30 years ago, that did not happen. The relationship between a patient and a doctor was more fulfilling for both the doctor and the patient.
We now have political Parties, and 1 put the NDP and the Liberal Party in this category, that view health care as an issue of labour relations and promote models that will lead to assembly line type care in a profession which requires commitment to people. The Government chooses to intrude on the lives of Canadians, patients as well as practitioners, by tackling one tiny part of the accessibility concern and not the most critical part. It chooses to tackle it by saying that it will fine or double tax those people in the province who do not do what the Government tells them they must do. If the Government is going to do that, the thought of the quality of health care professionals I am likely to encounter 10 or 20 years from now scares me to death.
The Government must be willing to try to counterbalance that provision with a provision which will provide some sense of equity and fairness for current and future professionals in the field. If there is no assurance for individuals who choose to enter health care professions that they will be treated equitably, fairly and will be allowed to practise their profession in a caring and compassionate manner, then how can any of us in the chamber encourage the best and brightest of our young people to choose this kind of a profession? How can any of us deal with our children who may be 18, 19 or 20 years of age by saying to them that they should go to school and study medicine, nursing or physiotherapy? How can we say that to them in all good conscience if we also say to them that a group of civil servants and politicians who they will never meet or influence are going to tell them how to do their job, not because that group has any training or experience, but simply because society gives it the power to do so? That is what is wrong, Mr. Speaker.
What is wrong with the approach taken by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to medicare in the country is that she has no compassion for or understanding of the long-range need for qualified, bright and compassionate people to serve their fellow human beings as health care professionals. She is in danger of doing more damage to the potential of our health care system in the long run than perhaps she really imagines. The House resumed consideration of Bill C-3, an Act relating to cash contributions by Canada in respect of insured health services provided under provincial health care insurance plans and amounts payable by Canada in respect of extended health care services and to amend and repeal certain acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

Motion No. 5
That Bill C-3 be amended in Clause 15 by striking out line 31 at page 11 and substituting the following therefor:
"made, and said order shall not come into force unless it is affirmed by a
resolution introduced and passed in accordance with the rules of those
Houses."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment is symbolic, shall we say, of a number of amendments I moved in committee, all of which, if accepted, would have had the effect of providing more parliamentary accountability in the process by which the Government of Canada, within the context of the Bill, could have reduced transfer payments to provinces which were not meeting program conditions other than those concerning extra billing and user fees.
As we know, where violations exist concerning extra billing and user fees there is a non-discretionary formula of a dollar for dollar. What we, and a number of people, were concerned about, as well as witnesses who came before the committee, was that with respect to other criteria there was too much authority given to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) to decide on what the penalty would be to any particular province.
In committee I suggested that instead of the matter being referred by the Minister of National Health and Welfare to the Governor in Council and Cabinet, if the Minister arrived at a judgment that a province was violating principles of accessibility, portability, provision of information, visibility, or whatever, that the matter be referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs. In that way Parliament would have an opportunity through one of its committees to look into whatever judgments were being made about a particular province's health care plan by the Minister of National Health and Welfare.
This would have had two effects: First, it would provide a forum in which provinces could go beyond the limited opportunities provided to them for dialogue between themselves and the federal Government with respect to whether they were violating the principles of medicare. It would have provided a forum where their case could have been heard. Presumably, if the provinces had a half decent case, there would be at least one Member of Pariament, or one political party, willing to put its case before the committee. There would be an opportunity for the principles of natural justice to be observed and for the provinces to have more of a hearing than they will get in the process provided for in the Bill as it stands.
Second, Mr. Speaker, I believe such an amendment would go a long way toward meeting some of the objectives which were set out for the future of Parliament by the Special Committee on Standing Orders and Procedures, which were, and I feel rightly so, that more power should be in the hands of parliamentarians and in the hands of committees of this House, and less power in the hands of cabinet, the Governor in Council and individual Ministers. This amendment would meet that kind of concern, Mr. Speaker.
Instead of this kind of one authority versus another, the Minister of National Health and Welfare versus the ten provincial ministers of health, or a particular Minister of Health, there could be a Committee of the House of Commons involved in the process. This amendment provides that in the final analysis, if the Minister wants to make a reduction in a federal transfer payment to a province, the Minister simply cannot do that by fiat. The Minister would have to do that with the approval of Parliament. This is what this amendment is all about, Mr. Speaker. I believe that all who are concerned about increasing the accountability of cabinet, the Prime Minister's Office and bureaucracy in general-and federal-provincial relations, for that matter-to Parliament, can see in this amendment an opportunity to advance that particular perception. I hope that I will receive support from Hon. Members on those grounds.

He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment addresses the very heart of the Bill because this is the crunch, really, as to whether these penalties will have the effect of actually eliminating extra billing and user fees. As has been said so many times, this is one of the few things which the Bill sets out to do.
We and everyone who supports the Bill have to ask whether or not these penalties will in fact result in the Provinces moving to eliminate extra billing, either by agreement with the medical professions or simply by imposing one regime or another. 1 kind of go from optimism to pessimism to optimism to pessimism. My first judgment was that for Provinces like Ontario and Alberta, where it so happens that we have the biggest extra billing problem, the penalties as they now stand are fiscally insignificant. The Provinces could decide to absorb these penalties if they felt ideologically attached enough to extra billing and user fees. The hope was that these penalties might be politically significant, that political criticism from within the Province of a Government which consistently chose to forfeit the revenues represented by the penalties in order to meet the needs of a minority of doctors would at some point become unbearable, and action would be taken against extra billing and user fees. That is still possible. What we are concerned about, which leads to my fluctuating view of a happy outcome, is that recently we have seen the Ontario Minister of Finance, Mr. Grossman, predicting that there will be an increase in Ontario taxes and OHIP premiums, or several other effects flowing from the penalties imposed on Ontario through this Bill. But none of the effects he has speculated upon have anything to do with the elimination of extra billing.
We already know the position of the Minister of Health in Alberta. He defends extra billing and user fees as an extension of his free enterprise view of reality. He sees all of this in somewhat the same vein as the National Citizens' Coalition, that it is part of the creeping communist conspiracy.
Canada Health Act
I think this is a legitimate concern about the penalties. 1 am sorry it has not been shared by the Government or by my Progressive Conservative colleagues, with whom I have had an opportunity to collaborate on a number of amendments. I realize when it comes to penalties that we in the NDP are alone in this respect and alone in this amendment.
We propose that a Province which continues to allow extra billing and user fees be penalized in an escalating fashion. After the first year, when you have a dollar for dollar penalty, we then go to a $2 for $1 penalty in the second year and a $3 for $1 penalty in the third year, and that it stay that way until something is done.
We have left in the three-year period of grace so that if the Province of Ontario, after its three-year agreement with the doctors has expired, wanted to put an end to extra billing it could get all its money back. There is no problem there. The increased penalties would not be permanent if there was the political will in Ontario to find a solution.
We agree with the perceptions of several of the witnesses who came before the committee, notably the Canadian Health Coalition and others, who think that the penalties are too light. 1 realize the Government feels that if it had more than a dollar for dollar penalty, it would be crossing some kind of political quasiconstitutional line, and it is not willing to go beyond a dollar for dollar penalty. The Government never really made available to Members of the Committee or this House the specific advice or judgment on which it based its opposition to the notion of escalating penalties. But I say to the Minister of National Health and Welfare that if she really expects the Canada Health Act to work, something in the order of escalating penalties would have been well advised in combination with what I suggested in motion No. 7, which was ruled out of order, that of some kind of positive incentive to Provinces who want to clean up their act with respect to extra billing and user fees. You would have a carrot approach for those Provinces who wanted to respond to the national consensus against extra billing and user fees, and a more effective stick for those Provinces you already know do not want to respond and are going to find every way they can not to respond. They are simply hoping that at some point in the future they will find a federal Government more friendly to their perceptions of how the health care system works. 1 hope that will never be the case. I hope that the consensus we have seen in the last two or three months against extra billing and user fees will hold.
I hope the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) will continue to speak for health care for the Progressive Conservatives and not the Hon. Member from Calgary and others who have spoken today and indicated the more traditional Tory line on these matters. I sometimes wonder how they are ever going to get it together and get up and vote for the Bill, because when you listen to them they sound like they are speaking against it.
I recommend these penalties, Mr. Speaker, as I have before, albeit futilely, to Members of the Government and my Progressive Conservative colleagues. I want to put on the record once again our concern that these penalties as they stand, in the

absence of any positive incentives and the willingness by the Minister to reopen the question of federal funding, are likely not going to work, and somewhere down the line we are going to have to have this debate all over again.
Hon. Monique Begin (Minister of National Health and
Welfare): Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Birds Hill (Mr. Blaikie), he is suggesting a bit of overkill. We have no proof it will work. After all, the purpose of this new Canada Health Act is to have legislation which can be implemented and which will effectively ban forever extra billing and user fees. The purpose of the Act is not to be punitive without reason. Although I have no special legal training, it has always appeared to me as a legislator, together with my colleagues in this House, that any piece of legislation not only must be fair but must be seen as having a clear element of fairness and equity if people are to have any respect for the legislation. If you think of this measure from the practical point of view, then the same holds true. Let me explain what I mean.
The existing legislation permits the federal Minister of National Health and Welfare to apply a very serious financial penalty to provinces where extra billing or user fees exist, denying accessibility. We have not been able to use it-let us call things by their name-because of several factors, one of them being that the penalties are so big. Just to refresh the memory of my colleagues, it must be equivalent to the total monthly cash money transfer from the federal Government to the Provinces. The penalty is so big that it could easily result in a disruption of services in the province involved. Then we would not have achieved what we wanted to achieve. Just the opposite. We could create a very serious backlash against the whole institution of medicare. So that everyone could be accused of causing a fatal accident which might not have anything to do with a service or an emergency department, or what not, being closed down by the provincial authorities in retaliation for the withholding of federal funding. All of that because the penalty is much too big. We believe that we are offering something very fair and operational. The penalty on extra billing and user fees must be big enough to mean something to the provincial authorities; something to push them into banning extra billing and user fees on the one hand, but not so big as to easily call for retaliation and disruption of services to Canadian patients. That is why we thought the concept of a dollar for a dollar was very fair.
I do know, but perhaps the Hon. Member needs a holiday. I am no doctor, but he said he goes up and down, he is optimistic and pessimistic. He either needs a tranquilizer of some sort or a holiday, otherwise why would he say things like that? Perhaps he needs a doctor who will not extra bill him.
Getting back to a more serious tone, I do not understand why he worries so much. The way the penalty works no provicial authority can make money out of the system. They can have no incentive whatsoever to let extra billing continue, or to institute user fees themselves. That is what we want.
In addition, I would not in terms of fairness be able to accept an escalation of penalty over three years. Some of the provinces have contractual agreements with their medical associations that exceed one year. Some have two year agreements. To my knowledge, one has a three year agreement. I believe that should be respected. The purpose is not to get at a province. The purpose is to make sure that medicare gets back to what it was intended for when it was created by this Parliament and to get rid of a bad habit which developed in recent years in the system, namely, overcharges to patients via extra billing by doctors and specialists, or user fees from the provinces. That is the purpose.
I think it is only fair to give the provinces a chance. This is an explicit clarification of the rules of the game. Many of them have already indicated that they will respect the new legislation of this Parliament and will, either all at once, or over the three years allowed, correct the situation that exists in their own provincial governments. That is the purpose of the Bill.
We cannot be pessimistic because a given provincial health Minister announces that he will first fix a certain part of the problem and then address another dimension of the extra charges in his province. We cannot be pessimistic about most provinces of Canada. Knowing how Canada functions, I believe that it will set the tone. Except for two provinces I believe all provinces will fully apply the spirit of this Bill and do away with the extra billing and user fee situation within the first three years.
Whenever they do so, as long as it is within the three years, they will immediately be reimbursed the amount of the penalty which was withheld from them. Of course we will not pay interest on it. However, the intention is to give them back exactly what was withheld from them. As my colleague said, they will have had the stick applied to them.
However, the Bill is not punitive and simply attempts to consolidate medicare. If the situation of overcharging is corrected in the first three years after the passage of this legislation, which will be deemed to be passed as of April 1, that money will definitely be reimbursed to them.

Mr. Speaker, I shall be very brief. In my mind Motion No. 6 does not address the central issue. The central issue is the withholding for a three year period of moneys equivalent to the extra billing or user fees which have been charged in the province. Hopefully during that three year period there will be an agreement made to enable the provinces to receive the full amount of money they are entitled to under the established programs financing. In my mind this motion is punitive, Mr. Speaker. I do not think it addresses the issue at all. It is for that reason I will be voting against it.

subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REGISTERED CHARITIES- DEPARTMENT'S INTERPRETATION-CHURCHES' OPPOSITION TO DIVORCE LEGISLATION
NATIONAL REVENUE-REGISTERED CHARITIES- DEPARTMENT'S INTERPRETATION-CHURCHES' OPPOSITION TO DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at times even I am amazed at what can happen in this House, and this is one of those times. When everything seems to be going in the opposite direction, suddenly by some great stroke of luck everyone starts agreeing again.
The point I want to raise relates to a question I asked in the House respecting the operations of Revenue Canada. Members are aware of the difficulty Revenue Canada has in its dealings with Canadians; its arbitrary measures, its use of garnishee orders. But the point I want to concentrate on today is as onerous as anything which has been brought before this House in the last month.
In order for members of organizations such as churches to get a receipt for the purpose of tax deductions in the amount of donations made, there is a 20 per cent maximum limit on the amount of income which can be receipted. There has always been a debate as to what is a legitimate activity of a church, which is a registered charity. Over these last years there has been an arbitrary approach, by which the Department of National Revenue says that a church can only be involved in activities which are exclusively "for charitable
March 26, 1984

purposes", and that it devote its resources exclusively to charitable activities.
The question then comes up as to whether a church violates its status as a registered charity if it gets involved in opposition to legislation. 1 will be specific. Presently on the Order Paper of the House is Bill C-10, an Act to Amend the Divorce Act. Many churches in Canada are opposed to the provisions of the Divorce Act. Some of their members and some of their leaders have signed petitions against the Divorce Act. They have spoken out from their pulpits and in public forums against the Act. If they do that are they violating their status as a registered charity? In my mind the answer is no.
I have a letter in hand addressed to the Pentecostal Assemblies of Canada signed by one Miss A. A. Conway, dated March 1, 1984. The pertinent paragraph reads as follows:
We would comment that in our view while it would be acceptable for a religious organization to take a public stand on a moral issue, it would not be acceptable for that organization to engage in a campaign designed to bring pressure to bear upon a government to implement legislative changes or adopt a policy which the organization advocates.
Those words are frightening, Mr. Speaker. It is saying that if the church recognizes that there is a moral issue they can say so. That is always what churches and their adherents have done. That is one of their responsibilities to society. They are to be the leaven in society, as are their members. However, if a Bill flows from this House that is in conflict with the moral issues for which that church stands, then that church is in violation of the regulations under which it was registered as a registered charity. In my mind, Mr. Speaker, that is a violation - of religious freedom.
Surely this country is better off when churches, their leaders and their adherents speak out against moral decay. Surely the country is better off when legislation which comes before the House is assessed by churches from a moral viewpoint. Surely law that comes here is not neutral, only legal, and has no moral consequences.
However, that is how this paragraph is now interpreted. I do not know if the Government really wants to follow up on that kind of interpretation from Revenue Canada. If it does, and if it does not clarify it today, I will tell them one thing. There are many people in the country who will see that kind of an interpretation as a direct attack on religious freedom and a direct attack upon what churches should be doing.
I will remind Hon. Members of a Bill which was before this House, C-10, through which churches were to be registered and were to give certain information regarding their membership. In fact, if a member was asked to leave that congregation, that ex-member could then go to the courts to ask for redress and, in fact, reinstatement. Is this another intrusion by the state on what I believe is legitimate activity by the church?
I ask the Parliamentary Secretary to clarify if the Government feels that it is not a legitimate practice for churches to take an active stand against or for legislation which, in their assessment, has moral implications? If churches are only
Adjournment Debate
supposed to act on what are exclusively charitable activities, how does the Government define charitable activities? What is the definition of a charitable activity? I think that all of us could agree on some, but what is the definition? I believe it is incumbent upon the Government to clarify this issue.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. Kenneth Robinson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: NATIONAL REVENUE-REGISTERED CHARITIES- DEPARTMENT'S INTERPRETATION-CHURCHES' OPPOSITION TO DIVORCE LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Provencher (Mr. Epp) is a very persuasive member, and I must say that he has almost persuaded me and others with his eloquent argument. However, I must say also that the law is the law, is the law. Mr. Bumble, in the Pickwick Papers, said that the law is an ass. Maybe it is. Maybe it is in this case as well and is something we must look at.
Having said that, the matter raised by the Hon. Member relates to the larger question of the incompatibility, for purposes of tax administration, between political activity and registration as a charity. It is a question which has been covered more than once in the House, possibly even in these proceedings, but I shall be happy to assist the Hon. Member at the risk of what may seem to be repetition to others.
Under the Income Tax Act, a registered charity must be constituted and operated exclusively for charitable purposes. However, the Act does not define charity. The Hon. Member raised this. We must therefore rely on the courts and that is where we come to the law. Perhaps it is time we provided a proper definition, or a clarification of charity and what the interpretation should be. That has not yet been done. Perhaps it is a job for Members of Parliament. Do not blame the courts for doing the job the way they see it at the present time.
The courts have said in particular that political activity is not charitable in nature, and have also concluded that efforts to procure a change in legislation can be considered to be political in nature. I must say that this appears to be stretching the point a bit. Once again, I think further clarification is necessary from Parliament.
In the circumstances as they presently exist, the Department has no choice but to decline to accept for registration as a charity an organization with political objects. In addition, any organization already registered as a charity under the Act is putting that status at risk when it engages in political activity. Perhaps it is necessary to explain as well what we mean by "political activity". I find it rather doubtful that what the Hon. Member is talking about is, in itself, political activity per se.
I am sure that the Hon. Member in these and other circumstances would want the Department to administer the law at this time as it has been interpreted by the courts. We must follow the law and that is all we can do. I hope that satisfies the Hon. Member at this time.

March 26, 1984
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-COSTS OF CANADA LANDS EXPLORATION-OIL SANDS POTENTIAL
NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-COSTS OF CANADA LANDS EXPLORATION-OIL SANDS POTENTIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week I addressed a question to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). I asked him how he could justify spending $12 billion on PIP grants for development in high risk exploration. I am talking about the offshores, in the tundra and the far north. His answer, as reported at page 2283 of Hansard was that:
Helping industries carry out exploration in Canada's North and off the coasts of Newfoundland and Nova Scotia is of fundamental importance to Canada because we must know what our resources are and how much our petroleum and natural gas reserves are worth, if we are to ensure self-sufficiency and security of supply-
I am not denying for a moment that getting an inventory of the oil and gas reserves we have in Canada Lands or on the offshore is of fundamental importance.
Clearly the Minister is evading the question because basically we are not going to achieve oil and gas self-sufficiency. The practise of the Government, through its National Energy Program and the PIP grant system taking taxpayers' money in the form of the petroleum gas revenue tax, and transferring it directly in the form of grants, totalling $12 to $14 billion since the implementation of the National Energy Program, is totally ludicrous. To suggest that there is not another way to gather the information and get the inventory in place in Canada Lands and in the off-shore is silly. Activity was going on offshore and in Canada Lands. The large companies were ready to gamble and take the risk. All we had to do was put the proper incentives in place to allow these companies to go ahead.
In northeastern Alberta we have the Athabasca Tar Sands which contain the single largest known oil reserve in the world. We have that in Canada, and we have the technology in place to extract the oil from those oil sands. We have the qualified people to do it. One single plant would create 30,000 to 40,000 jobs across the country. Why are we not focussing the attention on our oil sands? I made this suggestion to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien). He indicated that he had signed agreements on three small plants in northeastern Alberta, the in situ plant at Cold Lake and two others. They are relatively small but work is going ahead, not because of the National Energy Program but in spite of it.
The National Energy Program completely killed oil sands activity. The Minister is now modifying the Program by removing some of the onerous taxes on these plants and is allowing them to go ahead. It has been proved conclusively, by the millions of dollars that are now being expended around Bonnyville, Cold Lake and Grand Centre, on the Wolf Lake and the Cold Lake projects, that when the Government removed the restrictive taxes put in place through the National Energy Program exploration would go ahead.
William Hopper, President of Petro-Canada, announced as recently as last week that Petro-Canada is prepared to go ahead with a mining operation north of Fort McMurray if this Government removes some of the restrictive taxes that are in
place under the National Energy Program. He made that very clear.
I say to the Government, put the incentives in place and the companies will develop the oil sands. I say put the incentives in place and the major companies will explore the off-shore off Newfoundland, in the Arctic Circle, in the tundra and in the so-called Canada Lands.
Let me remind Hon. Members of the original discovery at Leduc No. 1 in 1947. Prior to that major companies came to Canada, invested money, explored for oil and drilled dry hole after dry hole. They were doing what is called wildcatting. They finally struck oil. At that point in 1947 there was not one Canadian oil company of substance in Canada-not one. We did not have drilling companies, seismic crews or companies, mud companies, logging companies, nor any of the multitude of companies that service the oil industry. Today these types of companies are close to 100 per cent Canadian owned because the companies that were encouraged to take the risk had the funds behind them to do so.
I say the Canadian taxpayer should not be paying $12 billion to $14 billion over the life of this National Energy Program to drill in high-risk exploration when we have oil sands ready to be developed. The same encouragement should be given to Canadian companies today. It would create activity and jobs across the country. This is just silly. We should be encouraging the majors to do it because they have the wherewithal, not enticing small Canadian companies to go into the offshore and the Arctic. When it comes to production time the small Canadian companies do not have the financial backing to enable them to put the oil onstream if and when they find it.
Hon. Members should remember that we have the largest, single, known oil reserve in Canada in the Athabasca tar sands. We have the people, we know where it is. We need it for energy self-sufficiency, but we are going to lose the opportunity that we have.

speakeroldname: Mr. Leonard Hopkins (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: NATIONAL ENERGY PROGRAM-COSTS OF CANADA LANDS EXPLORATION-OIL SANDS POTENTIAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in his question of March 21 concerning the costs of Canada Lands exploration, the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) referred to expenditures of taxpayers' dollars on high-risk exploration in the amount of $12 billion by 1986. For the record, I would like to point out that the forecast of expenditure under the Petroleum Incentives Program for the period January 1, 1981 to the end of 1986 is $8 billion on all lands in Canada. This includes payments under the program for Alberta, financed by the government of that province, which, together with Petroleum Incentives Program payments for programs in other provinces, account for close to 30 per cent of the total program. Consequently, Canada Lands exploration will receive something in the order of $5.6 billion over the period 1981-1986, not $12 billion. There will be an equal distribution of the $5.6 billion between Canada Lands in the north and off the East Coast.
March 26, 1984

Turning to the Hon. Member's objective of generating thousands of jobs through oil sands development, the primary purpose of oil exploration and development is to open up the country's oil resource potential for present and future generations. The extent to which this primary objective generates jobs is a very welcome consequence and, in this connection, Canada Lands exploration is producing jobs in areas where they are badly needed, particularly in the Atlantic provinces.
The argument is sometimes made that we should put all of our effort into the oil sands because the oil is there and the technology is known. The fact is that oil sands development is not without its risks and, in the matter of technology, reference could be made to a recently published statement by C. W. Bowman, head of the Alberta Oil Sands Technology and Research Authority, who said: "-in spite of progress to date, further quantum jumps in technology will be required before the full impact of the oil sands is realized".
The policy of this Government is to proceed on all fronts in working toward the objective of oil self-sufficiency. The results off the Newfoundland and Nova Scotia coasts have demonstrated the value of this approach.
At the same time, federal policy is very actively directed to oil sands and heavy oil development. The federal Government operates major incentives for the opening up of these resources including the provision of earned depletion allowance, relief from the Petroleum and Gas Revenue Tax, the world oil price, and special provisions to encourage heavy oil processing and marketing. The fact that the Cold Lake, Wolf Lake, and Elk Point oil sands projects are underway is evidence of the effectiveness of these measures, and of the royalty reduction provisions of the provinces. Other similar projects will not be long in coming.
In these brief comments, Mr. Speaker, I have emphasized the importance of an integrated program of oil resource development. Results show that it is paying off in terms of new resources while at the same time generating economic benefits for regions most in need.
